title: BERISHA AND HALJITI v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
summary: In Berisha and Haljiti v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicants, Dzavit Berisha and Baljie Haljiti, are nationals of Serbia and Montenegro of Balkan Egyptian origin—a group included within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Their case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Balkan Egyptian minorities in Kosovo, particularly the threats, harassment, and discrimination they faced due to their ethnicity and Mr. Berisha’s involvement in Roma rights advocacy. After marrying in 1999, the couple fled escalating violence in Kosovo, including threats of rape and forced expulsion by the Kosovo Liberation Army, and sought refuge in Macedonia. Despite repeated asylum applications, Macedonian authorities rejected their claims, finding their fears insufficiently substantiated, and ultimately expelled them after a failed attempt to cross into Greece. The applicants alleged violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 (prohibition of collective expulsion), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 6 (right to a fair trial), citing both the risk of persecution upon return and procedural shortcomings in the asylum and expulsion process. The European Court of Human Rights declared most complaints inadmissible, finding no evidence that the Macedonian authorities had failed to consider their individual circumstances or that the expulsion amounted to inhuman treatment. This case highlights the persistent challenges faced by Roma and Balkan Egyptian minorities in seeking protection from ethnic violence and underscores the importance of effective asylum procedures in the context of post-conflict Kosovo.
